title: From Principle to Practice: Lessons I have learnt about Implementing Lesson Principles Well
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Hughes shares what she learned implementing a trust-wide set of research-informed lesson principles, arguing that publishing a framework is only the beginning and that the harder work is achieving reliable classroom enactment. She applies the Education Endowment Foundation's explore-prepare-deliver-sustain implementation model, warning schools they can become 'very efficient at solving the wrong problem' if they skip careful diagnosis in the explore phase, and that an 'implementation dip' during first use is a normal part of learning rather than evidence the strategy has failed. She distinguishes lesson principles, instructional routines, and exemplification/coaching as three separate layers requiring leaders to be 'tight' on core components but 'looser' on subject-specific exemplification. Notably, she discloses that her own trust chose not to implement a whole-trust instructional coaching model despite her expertise, because the culture and systems needed to sustain it had to be built first.
points: Hughes structures her implementation lessons around the EEF's explore-prepare-deliver-sustain model, giving readers a research-grounded framework rather than a purely personal reflection.
Her warning that schools can become 'very efficient at solving the wrong problem consistently' names a specific risk of skipping the diagnostic explore phase before adopting new practices.
Her disclosure that her own trust deliberately delayed whole-trust instructional coaching, despite her own expertise in the area, models the discipline of 'not yet' over blanket rollout.

She distinguishes three implementation layers - lesson principles, instructional routines, exemplification/coaching - arguing leaders should be tight on core components but loose on subject-specific adaptation.
quotes: Too often, lesson principles are treated as if their publication is the main achievement: write the framework, share the slides, run a launch event, and expect practice to shift. In reality, that is only the beginning.

Schools can become very efficient at solving the wrong problem consistently. A playbook may be coherent and polished, but if it is not addressing a genuine need, or if it is not feasible in context, implementation will struggle from the start.

In my own trust for example, despite my expertise in instructional coaching, we decided not to implement a whole-trust instructional coaching approach - quite simply because the culture and systems to do it well needed to be crafted first.
There is often an implementation dip in which confidence falls and practice becomes uneven. This should not be interpreted as evidence that the strategy is wrong.
In the end, trust-wide consistency comes not from implementing everything at once, but from implementing fewer things more deeply.
